prime.problem: "Fewest buses", "fewest jumps", "fewest dice rolls": every one asks for a shortest hop count. A depth-first walk finds a path but can't tell you it is the shortest without trying them all.
prime.fits: Third graph card. The flood-fill card's stack becomes a queue, and the order of visiting, which didn't matter for filling, now carries the answer. Bus Routes also shows that choosing the graph matters as much as the search.
expect: stops ↔ buses as a two-kind graph
prime.goal: Model a "fewest moves" problem as nodes and unit-cost edges, run BFS layer by layer, and argue why the first arrival is the shortest.

attend: Why can the queue hold at most two layer numbers at once, and why does that make the first arrival the shortest?
In Bus Routes, why are the buses themselves nodes, instead of linking every pair of stops on a route?
Why is each bus boarded at most once, and what would happen to the running time without the used_buses set?
What goes wrong if you put the edge weights back on the course's graph and still run BFS?

must: Queue is first-in first-out → all nodes at distance d leave before any at d + 1 → a node's first discovery is along a fewest-hop path → mark it seen then and never revisit
Model stops and buses as nodes → a route of L stops costs L links instead of L(L − 1) stop-to-stop edges → 100,000 vs 9,999,900,000 for one long route → BFS runs in O(S) total

BFS counts hops, not cost → correct only when every edge costs the same → on the weighted course graph it returns A-C-E (cost 12) while the cheapest is 10 → weights need Dijkstra; 0/1 weights need 0-1 BFS
elevated: Processing a whole frontier list per iteration (instead of popping one node at a time) makes the layer number a loop counter → the answer is just how many layers you expanded
reference: the Snakes and Ladders board numbering
the source's use of dijkstra with unit weights

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the stop ↔ bus graph for routes = [[1, 2, 7], [3, 6, 7]], mark the layers from stop 1, and write two sentences on why the answer is 2 and why BFS guarantees it is minimal.
checklist: layer 1: bus 0 reaches stops 2, 7; layer 2: bus 1 reaches 3, 6
the target 6 appears in layer 2, so 2 buses
FIFO order: every node at distance d is found before any at d + 1
seen/used sets make each stop and each bus processed once: O(S)

retrieve.q: Explain the invariant that makes BFS's first arrival a shortest path, in terms of what the queue can contain.
answer: the queue holds nodes of distance d followed by nodes of distance d + 1, never more than two values
a node found from u gets dist[u] + 1, and u left in layer order
so no later discovery can be shorter than the first

retrieve.q: Trace Jump Game III from index 5 on arr = [4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 1, 2]: list each layer and say when the search stops.
One route has 100,000 stops. Compare modelling Bus Routes with stop-to-stop edges against the stop ↔ bus graph: edges, running time, and what you give up.
answer: stop ↔ bus: 100,000 links, each route scanned once
the only cost is a second kind of node, and the layer count must count buses not stops

compare.q: Dijkstra with every weight 1 gives BFS's answers. What does the heap do that the queue doesn't need to, and what does that cost?
answer: the heap orders by distance; with unit weights FIFO order already is distance order
BFS: O(V + E); Dijkstra: O((V + E) log V)
use the heap only when weights differ

compare.q: Both visit every reachable node once in O(V + E). Which question can only one of them answer, and which one can each answer that the other can't do as naturally?
answer: BFS: fewest hops, because of layer order
DFS: finishing order, which topological sort and cycle detection use
for plain filling or counting regions, either works

predict.q: Snakes and Ladders on a plain 6 × 6 board with no snakes or ladders: predict the fewest rolls from square 1 to 36 before running BFS.
predict.answer: 6 rolls. You need to advance 35 squares and a roll moves at most 6, so at least ⌈35/6⌉ = 6 rolls, and BFS confirms 6 (it's 4 on LeetCode's example 1 because a ladder skips ahead). With no special squares the graph is just a line with jumps of up to 6, so the layers are ranges of squares.

apply.task: Run the Jump Game III BFS by hand from start = 0 on arr = [4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 1, 2], writing each layer. Then run Bus Routes on LeetCode's example 2, routes = [[7,12],[4,5,15],[6],[15,19],[9,12,13]], source 15, target 12, and explain the result from the graph.
apply.done: Jump Game: layers [0], [4], [1], [3], so True after 3 jumps. Bus Routes returns −1: stop 15's buses (1 and 3) reach only 4, 5, 15, 19, and no bus from those reaches 12.
apply.hint: For the bus case, list which buses serve each stop first; the BFS dies when a layer adds no new stop.
